docs.title: Signified
docs.text:
A fast, fully-typed Python library for reactive programming.

$ uv add signified

docs.title: Values that reactively stay up to date
docs.text:
Ordinary Python assignment takes a snapshot:

price = 10
quantity = 2
total = price * quantity  # 20

quantity = 3
print(total)  # still 20

total holds the number that price * quantity produced at that moment. If price or quantity change, you have to remember to recalculate total, along with anything calculated from total, and anything else calculated using those values. In a large program, that bookkeeping can easily miss something.

Reactive programming removes that bookkeeping. You describe how values depend on one another and Signified works out what needs to be recalculated when an input changes.

docs.title: Signals
docs.text:
In Signified, a value you plan to change goes in a signal. When a calculation reads a signal, Signified records that the calculation depends on it, so changing the signal marks those results as out-of-date.

Here is the example above written with signals:

from signified import Signal

price = Signal(10)
quantity = Signal(2)
total = price * quantity

print(total.value)  # 20
quantity.value = 3
print(total.value)  # 30

price and quantity are signals. Multiplying them does not produce a number; it produces a Computed, a calculation that follows both inputs. Read any of them with .value, and change a signal by assigning to its .value.

docs.title: The building blocks
docs.text:
Type What it is Example Signal A value you can change the price, the quantity Computed A calculation that follows its inputs the total Effect An action that runs when the values it reads change printing the total Binding Like a signal, but it can also follow another reactive value, and you can switch what it follows without rebuilding the calculations that use it a shape's position: a fixed number now, an animation later

Python operators, attribute access, and method calls on reactive values create Computed values for you. For your own functions, use @computed:

from signified import Signal, computed

@computed
def with_tax(amount: float, rate: float) -> float:
    return round(amount * (1 + rate), 2)

price = Signal(10)
quantity = Signal(2)
tax_rate = Signal(0.08)

total = with_tax(price * quantity, tax_rate)
print(total.value)  # 21.6
tax_rate.value = 0.1
print(total.value)  # 22.0

@computed makes it so the function receives ordinary values and returns a reactive result, but callers can pass signals, computed values, or plain values.

Computed objects answer what a value is, but when something should happen on a change, use an effect. Effects run once immediately, then again whenever the values they depend on have changed:

from signified import effect

@effect
def show(total: float) -> None:
    print(f"Total: ${total:.2f}")

watcher = show(total)  # Total: $22.00
quantity.value = 5     # Total: $55.00
watcher.dispose()      # stop watching

docs.title: How updates happen
docs.text:
Signified tries to keep things simple:

  • Dependencies come from reads. A calculation depends on the reactive values it reads while it runs, and nothing else.
  • Calculations are lazy and cached. A Computed runs when its value is needed, then saves the result until one of its inputs changes.
  • Effects are for actions. When something should happen on a change, such as updating a display or writing a log, use an effect instead of a calculation.

How updates work covers these rules in detail, including equality, batching, and errors.

Signified also carries type hints through these expressions, so your editor knows that total.value is a float. For maximum compatibility, use Pyright. For more details on current limitations refer to the type checker guide.

docs.title: signified.Signal
docs.text:
Bases: Signal[T], Variable[T]

Mutable state.

Signal stores a value and notifies observers when that value changes. The value property is read/write:

  • reading value returns the exact stored value
  • assigning value updates the stored value and notifies observers if it changed

Assigning any other public attribute forwards the write to the wrapped object; see setattr.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default value T

Value to wrap.

required equal Callable[[T, T], bool] | None

Optional equal(previous, new) -> bool. When it returns True, an assignment counts as unchanged: the previous object is kept and observers are not notified. See also rx.with_equal.

None Example 
>>> count = Signal(1)
>>> doubled = count * 2
>>> doubled.value
2
>>> count.value = 3
>>> doubled.value
6

Attribute writes reach the wrapped object and notify observers:

>>> class Person:
...     def __init__(self, name: str):
...         self.name = name
...     def greet(self) -> str:
...         return f"Hi, I'm {self.name}!"
>>> s = Signal(Person("Alice"))
>>> result = s.greet()
>>> result.value
"Hi, I'm Alice!"
>>> s.name = "Bob"
>>> result.value
"Hi, I'm Bob!"

docs.title: at
docs.text:
at(value)

Temporarily set the signal to a given value within a context.

Restores the previous value when the context exits, even if an exception is raised.

The previous version is restored along with the previous value, so a dependent that was not read inside the context is not left needing a recompute. Dependents read inside the context recompute as usual. If the signal is written again inside the context, exit falls back to an ordinary assignment.

A Computed cannot change signals, so inside one at() raises RuntimeError unless value is the value the signal already holds. To read a value as if the signal held another value, use sample.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default value T

The temporary value to set.

required Example 
>>> s = Signal(1)
>>> with s.at(99):
...     print(s.value)
99
>>> s.value
1

docs.title: update
docs.text:
update()

Force a notification to all observers unconditionally.

Unlike assigning to .value, this does not check whether the stored value has changed. Use this when the contained object has been mutated in-place and change detection cannot detect the mutation (e.g. appending to a list stored in the signal).

Warning

Every downstream Computed that depends on this signal will recompute on its next .value read, even if the underlying data is unchanged. Prefer assigning to .value when possible.

docs.title: __setattr__
docs.text:
__setattr__(name, value)

Forward a public attribute write to the wrapped object and notify.

Private names and Signal's own attributes (such as value) are assigned on the wrapper. Any other name must already exist on the wrapped object; the write is applied there and observers are notified, exactly like signal[key] = value. Unknown names raise AttributeError instead of silently creating an attribute on the wrapper.

Only Signal forwards writes, because only a Signal owns its value. A Computed holds a cache that the next refresh replaces, so writing through it would mutate state it does not own.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default name str

The attribute name to assign.

required value Any

The value to assign.

required

Raises:

Type Description AttributeError

If the wrapped object has no attribute name.

>>> result = computed(sum)(s)
>>> result.value

>>> s[1] = 4
>>> result.value

docs.title: signified.Computed
docs.text:
Bases: Computed[T], Variable[T]

Reactive value derived from a computation.

Computed lazily re-runs its function and updates its value whenever a dependency changes. Dependencies are inferred automatically from which reactive values are read during evaluation.

In most cases Computed instances should be created implicitly by using overloaded operators or the computed decorator rather than directly using the Computed class.

Unlike Signal, Computed.value is read-only. Ordinary exceptions are cached like values and re-raised on reads until a dependency changes or invalidate() forces another evaluation.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default f Callable[[], T]

Zero-argument function used to compute the current value.

required equal Callable[[T, T], bool] | None

Optional equal(previous, current) -> bool. When it returns True, a recomputed value counts as unchanged: the previous object is kept and dependents are not invalidated. By default, built-in scalars compare by value and other objects by identity. Reads inside equal are not tracked, and an exception it raises is cached like an exception from f. See also rx.with_equal.

None Example 
>>> count = Signal(2)
>>> squared = Computed(lambda: count.value ** 2)
>>> squared.value
4
>>> count.value = 5
>>> squared.value
25

With equal, a new but equal result keeps dependents clean:

>>> count = Signal(2)
>>> parity = Computed(lambda: [count.value % 2], equal=lambda a, b: a == b)
>>> first = parity.value
>>> count.value = 4
>>> parity.value is first
True

docs.title: invalidate
docs.text:
invalidate()

Force a full recomputation on the next .value read.

Use this when a reactive attribute is replaced with a new object and the normal change-detection path may not pick up the change. Unlike a regular update, this always triggers re-evaluation regardless of whether dependencies appear unchanged.

Warning

This method is fragile and should be a last resort. Incorrect use can cause unnecessary recomputation or missed updates. Prefer assigning to .value whenever possible, as this triggers the standard change-detection path.

Example 
>>> external = {"value": 1}
>>> c = Computed(lambda: external["value"])
>>> c.value
1
>>> external["value"] = 99  # mutation not tracked by reactivity
>>> c.value  # still cached
1
>>> c.invalidate()
>>> c.value
99

docs.title: signified.Effect
docs.text:
Bases: Effect

Run a function now, and again whenever the reactive values it read change.

Each run records the reactive values fn reads, through .value or unref. A change to any of them runs fn again. Only reads from the latest run count: in Effect(lambda: x.value if flag.value else y.value), while flag is true, changing y does nothing.

The first run happens immediately, or when the enclosing batch exits. Several changes before a run share one run, and a run is skipped if nothing it read actually changed, such as a calculation that recalculated to the same result.

Warning

Keep a reference to the effect for as long as it should run. A discarded effect is garbage collected and stops:

Effect(lambda: print(s.value))      # runs once, then never again
e = Effect(lambda: print(s.value))  # runs on every change

Call dispose to stop it explicitly.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default fn Callable[[], None]

Zero-argument function to run for its side effects.

required Example 
>>> seen = []
>>> s = Signal(1)
>>> e = Effect(lambda: seen.append(s.value))
>>> seen
[1]
>>> s.value = 2
>>> s.value = 3
>>> seen
[1, 2, 3]
>>> e.dispose()
>>> s.value = 99
>>> seen
[1, 2, 3]

docs.title: The rx namespace
docs.text:
Every signal, computed value, and binding has an rx property. It holds reactive versions of operations that Python syntax can't make reactive, such as identity checks, membership, and choosing between two values:

Helper methods available under signal_or_computed.rx.

T is the source's value type and Source its exact reactive type, so helpers that return the source keep it as Signal, Computed, or Binding.

docs.title: effect
docs.text:
effect(fn)

Call fn with the source's value now, and again whenever it changes.

A shortcut for Effect(lambda: fn(source.value)). Inside batch, calls wait until the batch exits.

Keep the returned Effect for as long as fn should run, and call dispose to stop it.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default fn Callable[[T], None]

Called with the source's current value.

required

Returns:

Type Description 'Effect'

The Effect that calls fn.

Example 
>>> seen = []
>>> s = Signal(1)
>>> e = s.rx.effect(seen.append)
>>> seen
[1]
>>> s.value = 2
>>> s.value = 3
>>> seen
[1, 2, 3]
>>> e.dispose()
>>> s.value = 99
>>> seen
[1, 2, 3]

docs.title: tap
docs.text:
tap(fn)

Lazily call fn on evaluation and pass through the source value.

This returns a cached Computed: repeated reads without invalidation do not repeat the callback, and unread intermediate values are skipped. Keep the result alive. Use rx.effect for eager side effects, or untracked() to inspect a value without subscribing.

Example 
>>> seen = []
>>> s = Signal(1)
>>> passthrough = s.rx.tap(seen.append)
>>> s.value = 2
>>> seen
[]
>>> passthrough.value
2
>>> seen
[2]

docs.title: with_equal
docs.text:
with_equal(equal)

Set the custom equality the source uses to decide whether it changed.

When equal(previous, new) returns True, a new value counts as unchanged: the previous object is kept and dependents are not invalidated. This is the same as passing equal= to Signal or Computed, and also works on values built by operators, computed, and rx.map. It applies to later changes only. Pass None to restore the default (built-in scalars by value, other objects by identity).

The source is changed in place and returned, so the call can end an expression: m = (rotation @ scale).rx.with_equal(np.array_equal).

Example 
>>> source = Signal(1)
>>> parity = source.rx.map(lambda value: [value % 2]).rx.with_equal(lambda a, b: a == b)
>>> first = parity.value
>>> source.value = 3
>>> parity.value is first
True

Each time the result is calculated, every Signal, Computed, or Binding argument is replaced by its current value, so func receives plain values. Other arguments are passed as-is, including lists or dictionaries that hold reactive values; call deep_unref inside func to read those.

effect(func)

Make a function start an Effect each time it is called.

Arguments are handled as in computed: each Signal, Computed, or Binding argument is replaced by its current value, and other arguments are passed as-is.

The effect runs immediately, or when the enclosing batch exits, and again whenever a reactive value it read changes. Keep the returned Effect for as long as it should run.

>>> e = log(s)
>>> seen
[1]
>>> s.value = 2
>>> seen

>>> e.dispose()
>>> s.value = 3
>>> seen

docs.title: signified.batch
docs.text:
batch()

Defer effects until the outermost synchronous batch exits.

Writes are immediate and computed reads remain current. Newly created effects are deferred too. Nested batches combine; cascading writes may run an effect more than once. This is not a transaction: errors do not roll back writes, and ordinary reads can see intermediate state. A batch defers only work queued on the thread that entered it. Do not span await.

One failing effect raises its exception directly; several are raised as an ExceptionGroup. A body exception alone is re-raised unchanged; simultaneous body and flush failures are grouped together.

docs.title: signified.untracked
docs.text:
untracked()

Read without subscribing the enclosing computation or effect.

Nested computations still collect their own dependencies. Reads return current values and retain normal hooks and errors. Applies only to the thread that enters it; this context must not span await.

docs.title: signified.sample
docs.text:
sample(value, signal, at)

Return a Computed holding value as if signal held at.

Reading the result gives what reading value inside with signal.at(at): would give, without changing signal or any cached value. at may be reactive; it is read with signal's real value, then substituted.

The result recalculates when at changes, or when something value read other than signal changes. Changing only signal leaves it cached. Values that do not depend on signal are read as they are; values that do are calculated again for at, and the result keeps them.

Those values are calculated as on a first read, so a computed's custom equal has no earlier value to keep. Where Signal.at() would keep a cached value because equal accepts the new one, sample gives the new one, which that equal calls equal to it. This also means the result does not depend on what the live graph cached when it was read.

A Computed cannot change signals, including with Signal.at; use sample to read a value at another value of a signal.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default value HasValue[T]

The value to read.

required signal Signal[S]

The Signal to give another value.

required at HasValue[S]

The value signal holds while value is read.

required

Returns:

Type Description Computed[T]

A Computed of value as if signal held at.

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

If signal is not a Signal.

Example 
>>> frame = Signal(0)
>>> position = computed(lambda f: f * 10)(frame)
>>> held = sample(position, frame, 3)
>>> until = sample(position, frame, computed(lambda f: min(f, 3))(frame))
>>> frame.value = 2
>>> held.value, until.value
(30, 20)
>>> frame.value = 5
>>> held.value, until.value, position.value
(30, 30, 50)

docs.title: signified.tracked_fields
docs.text:
tracked_fields(cls: C) -> C

tracked_fields(*names: str) -> Callable[[C], C]

tracked_fields(*args)

Track reads and reassignment of a class's attributes.

Reading a tracked attribute returns exactly what was stored: a plain value, or the Signal, Computed, or Binding that was assigned. It never unwraps. Inside a computation or effect, the read also depends on the attribute itself, so assigning a new value invalidates the reader. Use unref as usual to read through a stored reactive value.

Assignment uses the usual change rule: built-in scalars compare by value, other objects by identity. Assigning a reactive value replaces the stored one; it never writes into the previously stored signal.

Apply it above @dataclass to track every field, or pass names to track only those. Names are required for a class that is not a dataclass. Both slotted and dict-based classes work; frozen dataclasses are rejected. Copies and pickles store plain values and get their own tracking.

Reads outside a computation skip the graph, but still cost a descriptor call. In-place mutation of a stored object is not observed.

Example 
>>> from dataclasses import dataclass
>>> from signified import HasValue, unref
>>> @tracked_fields
... @dataclass(slots=True)
... class Material:
...     roughness: HasValue[float] = 0.5
>>> material = Material()
>>> doubled = Computed(lambda: unref(material.roughness) * 2)
>>> doubled.value
1.0
>>> material.roughness = 0.25
>>> doubled.value
0.5
>>> material.roughness = Signal(0.1)
>>> doubled.value
0.2

docs.title: signified.deep_unref module-attribute
docs.text:
deep_unref

Replace reactive values inside nested containers with their current values.

For example, deep_unref({"x": Signal(1)}) returns {"x": 1}. Lists, tuples, dictionaries (keys and values), sets, frozensets, deques, and NumPy object arrays are rebuilt with their reactive contents replaced. Other objects are returned unchanged.

To support your own type, register a handler with @deep_unref.register(MyType). The handler receives the object and a resolve function (ResolveContext); call resolve on each field to read and return the rebuilt object. Only that exact type uses the handler, and registering the type again replaces it.

Called inside a computation or effect, every reactive value it reads becomes a dependency. Repeated references are resolved separately, cycles eventually raise RecursionError, and keys or set members that collide after resolving raise ValueError.

docs.title: signified.ResolveContext
docs.text:
Resolve a child within the current traversal.

Handlers call resolve(child) for each field they want to visit. The supplied context recursively resolves values with the current handlers.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text: This page summarizes notable changes across releases.

docs.title: sample()
docs.text:
sample(value, signal, at) returns a Computed holding value as if signal held at. Nothing else changes: not the signal, and not any cached value.

frame = Signal(0)
position = computed(lambda f: f * 10)(frame)

held = sample(position, frame, 3)  # position at frame 3, on every frame
until = sample(position, frame, computed(lambda f: min(f, 3))(frame))  # live, then held from frame 3
  • The result recalculates when at changes, or when something value reads other than signal changes. Changing only signal leaves it cached.
  • at may be reactive. It is read with the signal's real value, then substituted.
  • It works inside computeds, through branches, untracked(), Binding and native nodes, and samples can be nested.
  • Values are calculated as on a first read, so a computed's custom equal has no earlier value to keep. Where Signal.at() would keep a cached value that equal accepts, sample() gives the new one.
  • Reads cost nothing extra in a program that never calls sample().

Use Signal.at() to run code as if a signal held another value, and sample() to keep a value from another value of a signal.

docs.title: Breaking changes
docs.text:
• Breaking: A Computed can no longer change a signal while it is being evaluated. Doing so raises RuntimeError, which is cached like any other error from the function. Previously such a change could leave dependents stuck on an old value for good; for example, with frame.at(f): inside a computed froze everything downstream. The rule covers:

    • assigning .value or a tracked_fields attribute;
    • Signal.at() with a value other than the current one;
    • update(), invalidate(), item assignment, item deletion and attribute assignment on a Signal;
    • invalidate() on a Computed.

    It applies inside untracked() too, and in a custom equal or a plugin's updated hook while a computed is refreshing. Assigning the value a signal already holds is still allowed, as are writes from effects and from code outside computeds. Use sample() in place of Signal.at() inside a computed.

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text:
• A plugin's updated hook that raises no longer leaves dependents stale.
  • copy.copy() of a tracked_fields instance that keeps its fields in the instance dict now holds the values it was copied with.
  • A Computed with equal= no longer calls equal for a new result that the built-in rules already count as unchanged, such as a newly created int equal to the previous one. Signal already worked this way, as described in What counts as a change.

docs.title: Runtime improvements
docs.text:
• tracked_fields attributes are now read and written by a compiled descriptor. Reading a field outside a calculation is about three times faster, and assigning one about twice as fast.
  • Refreshing a computed value no longer copies its function and arguments first, which saves an allocation and reference-count updates on every refresh.

docs.title: Breaking changes
docs.text:
• Breaking: Signified's reactive engine is now a compiled extension written in Rust (signified._core). Signal, Computed, Binding and Effect keep their API, and most graphs update several times faster. Behavior changes:

    • A signal written twice while a change is propagating now notifies both times. Previously the second write could leave a dependent computed stale.
    • Subclasses can no longer override update() or value; defining either raises TypeError. Derive a Computed (for example with signal.rx.map(fn)) instead of overriding value.
    • copy.copy() and copy.deepcopy() of a Signal, Computed or Binding raise TypeError. Deep-copying a Computed previously produced an object that never updated. Instances using tracked_fields still copy and pickle.
    • Reading or writing a Signal whose __init__ was never called raises RuntimeError.
    • Breaking: subscribe(), unsubscribe(), and notify() on Signal, Computed, and Binding are now private. Use an Effect to react to changes.
    • Breaking: Removed signified.plugins.pm; use plugin_manager.
    • Breaking: Removed the migration warnings added in 0.6: signified.migration and SIGNIFIED_MIGRATION_WARNINGS. To check code written for 0.5, run the warnings on 0.6 before upgrading; see Migrating to 0.6.

docs.title: Runtime improvements
docs.text: • Each thread now tracks reads, batches, and effects on its own. Previously two threads using Signified at once, even with unrelated graphs, could raise RuntimeError: tracking frames are unbalanced, record a read on one thread as a dependency of a computation on another, or hold back each other's effects. Separate graphs can now run on separate threads, and a graph can be handed from one thread to another. Use one graph from one thread at a time: reading a Computed while another thread is computing it raises RuntimeError.

docs.title: Packaging
docs.text:
• Signified now ships a compiled extension, built with maturin. Wheels cover CPython 3.12 and later on Linux (x86_64 and aarch64, glibc and musl), macOS (Intel and Apple silicon), Windows x64, and Pyodide 314 (Python 3.14). Installing on other platforms builds from source and needs a Rust toolchain. Under Pyodide, a value more than 250 refreshes deep raises RecursionError, because the browser's stack is much smaller than a native one.
  • Plugin hooks run whenever a plugin is registered with plugin_manager; SIGNIFIED_ENABLE_HOOKS and signified.plugins.HOOKS_ENABLED are removed.
  • Plugins no longer use pluggy, and the plugins extra is removed. @hookimpl, plugin_manager.register, and plugin_manager.unregister work as before. register now rejects an @hookimpl method whose name is not a known hook, and no longer takes a name argument. pluggy options such as @hookimpl(tryfirst=True) and hook wrappers are not supported.
  • Removed the ipython extra. Notebook display works the same without it.

docs.title: Breaking changes
docs.text: • Breaking: Reactive objects no longer overload !=. Comparisons between reactive objects use identity and return a plain bool, matching ==. Replace (x != y) with x.rx.ne(y) for reactive value comparisons, alongside the existing x.rx.eq(y).

docs.title: Runtime improvements
docs.text:
• Added tracked_fields, a class decorator that makes reassigning an attribute invalidate computations that read it. Reads return the stored value unchanged. It works with slotted and dict-based dataclasses, or named attributes of other classes.
  • Signal and Computed accept equal=, a custom equality such as np.array_equal. When it reports a new value equal to the previous one, the previous object is kept and dependents are not invalidated. x.rx.with_equal(equal) sets it on an existing value, including values built by operators, computed, and rx.map, and returns that value.
  • Signal forwards item deletion (del signal[key]) to the wrapped list or dict and notifies observers, like signal[key] = value.
  • Signal.at() and Binding.at() restore the previous version as well as the previous value on exit. Dependents that were not read inside the with block no longer recompute afterwards.
  • other @ reactive, other << reactive, and other >> reactive now produce reactive values instead of raising TypeError.
  • Operators with a NumPy array on the left, such as array + reactive or array < reactive, now return one Computed instead of an array of Computed objects. Passing a reactive value straight to a ufunc, as in np.sin(reactive), now raises TypeError; use reactive.rx.map(np.sin).

docs.title: Type inference
docs.text:
Type checkers infer more precise results for reactive operators and helpers, and reject operations the wrapped type does not support.

  • Operators report the wrapped type's declared result, with the plain or reactive value on either side, instead of a union of the operand types. Built-in numbers follow Python's promotion rules, so Signal(1) / 2 is Computed[float]. Dates and datetimes subtract to timedelta, and adding or subtracting a timedelta keeps the date type.
  • abs, round, divmod, math.floor, math.ceil, math.trunc, and unary -, +, and ~ infer the declared result, such as Computed[int] for round(x) and Computed[Decimal] for round(decimal, 2).
  • Indexing keeps the item type, and slicing a list, tuple, or string with a reactive slice keeps the container type. rx.contains and rx.in_ reject containers that do not support membership.
  • rx.eq, rx.ne, and rx.as_bool keep custom and literal result types, so rx.where can narrow its result when the condition is known to be true or false.
  • as_rx, and rx helpers that return the source, such as rx.with_equal, keep the exact Signal, Computed, or Binding type.
  • Known gap: divmod(reactive, plain) loses its type when only the plain value's type defines __rdivmod__. Wrapping it in Signal restores inference.

• Added Binding for switching the source followed by existing calculations.
  • Added batch() to group writes before effects run, and untracked() to read values without adding dependencies.
  • Breaking: signals now store reactive objects as-is, and computed values can return them as-is. unref reads one reactive object at a time.
  • Breaking: decorated functions read direct reactive arguments only. Use deep_unref inside callbacks to read nested containers, and register custom iterable types to keep resolving their contents.
  • Change detection now compares exact built-in scalars by value and other objects by identity. Computations and effects skip work when their calculated inputs are unchanged, including after an equal-valued binding source change.
  • Computed values save ordinary exceptions until an input changes or they are explicitly invalidated. Failed runs track the inputs they reached and can recover.
  • Effects run after affected calculations are marked for refresh. Multiple effect failures are reported together as an ExceptionGroup.
  • Breaking: only Signal forwards attribute and item writes. Unknown attribute names raise AttributeError.
  • Removed rx.peek(fn); use rx.tap(fn).

See Migrating to 0.6 for required code changes and How updates work for the full behavior.

Add is_reactive to inspect wrappers without reading their values. Improve union inference for unref and as_rx; runtime resolution is unchanged.

Add deep_unref.register(Type) for custom containers and retain NumPy shape/dtype. Repeated references are resolved independently; cycles raise RecursionError. Resolved key/member collisions raise ValueError instead of silently discarding entries, and unhashable keys/members raise TypeError. Legacy traversal of unregistered iterables warns that it will be removed in 0.6.0.

Add opt-in migration diagnostics with migration.enable_warnings() or SIGNIFIED_MIGRATION_WARNINGS=1, including nested containers and safe cleanup when warnings are treated as errors. Existing resolution and propagation stay in place while applications identify affected patterns.

Add rx.tap(fn) for the lazy cached callback helper. rx.peek(fn) remains a deprecated alias until its removal in 0.6.0. Repeated cached reads do not rerun the callback; unread intermediate updates are skipped.

See Migrating to 0.6 for changes you can make on 0.5.1 and changes that require upgrading the runtime.

docs.title: Removals
docs.text:
The following deprecated APIs were removed. Their replacements are listed below.

Functions

  • reactive_method — use computed instead.
  • as_signal — use as_rx instead.

Arguments

  • Computed(fn, dependencies=...) — use Computed(fn) instead.

Public Methods

  • Variable.add_name — use Variable.with_name instead.
  • Variable.as_bool — use Variable.rx.as_bool instead.
  • Variable.contains — use Variable.rx.contains instead.
  • Variable.is_not — use Variable.rx.is_not instead.
  • Variable.eq — use Variable.rx.eq instead.
  • Variable.where — use Variable.rx.where instead.

Plumbing Methods

  • Variable.observe — use Variable._observe instead.
  • Variable.unobserve — use Variable._unobserve instead.

docs.title: @effect decorator
docs.text:
A new @effect decorator mirrors @computed, making it easy to define reactive side effects as plain functions:

@effect
def log(x):
    print(x)

e = log(some_signal)  # runs immediately, re-runs on change

Like @computed, arguments are automatically unwrapped, so the function always receives plain Python values. The effect stays active as long as you hold a reference to the returned Effect.

docs.title: Performance improvements
docs.text:
The internals were substantially reworked for speed:

  • Observer subscriptions are now stored as intrusive linked lists, reducing allocation overhead for high-fan-out signals.
  • Computed nodes reuse existing dependency links across re-evaluations instead of rebuilding them from scratch.
  • Invalidation uses a global version counter to short-circuit redundant recomputation in deep graphs.
  • Common cases in computed, effect, and other internal implementation details now have cheaper early-exit paths.

docs.title: Bug fixes
docs.text:
Fix bug causing __getattr__ to do infinite loops when the object attempts to be deep copied.

Make __setattr__ slightly more robust.

docs.title: Effect rework
docs.text:
Effect now auto-tracks its dependencies the same way Computed does. The constructor signature has changed: instead of taking a reactive source and a callback, it now takes a single zero-argument callable. Every reactive value read via .value or unref() inside that callable is automatically registered as a dependency.

# Before (0.3.0)
e = Effect(s, lambda v: print(v))

# After (0.3.1)
e = Effect(lambda: print(s.value))

Conditional branches are handled correctly — only the signals actually read during the most recent run are tracked, and the dependency set updates automatically when branches change.

docs.title: unref() now participates in dependency tracking
docs.text: Calling unref() inside a Computed or Effect evaluation now registers each unwrapped reactive as a dependency, the same as reading .value directly. Previously unref() bypassed tracking entirely.

docs.title: Invalidation API
docs.text: Added invalidate() to all reactive values. For Computed, pass force=True to bypass the dependency-version check and guarantee a full re-evaluation on the next read. Use this when the dependency topology changes outside the reactive graph (for example, replacing an object attribute that points to a signal or computed).

docs.title: Bug Fixes
docs.text:
• Fixed transient computed dependency retention: dependencies are now held strongly during evaluation, preventing them from being dropped by garbage collection before downstream updates complete.
  • Fixed exception rollback in Computed and Effect: if the user function raises, the previous dependency set and staleness state are preserved so the node retries correctly on the next change.

Breaking Changes

  • Effect constructor: the two-argument form Effect(source, fn) is gone. Replace with Effect(lambda: fn(source.value)).
  • NestedValue removed: from signified import NestedValue will raise ImportError. Use HasValue or ReactiveValue; explicit source chains use Binding.
  • Internal module renames: the private implementation modules have been reorganised. Any code importing directly from signified.core, signified.types, or signified.display will break. Use the public signified namespace instead.

Deprecations

  • as_signal(val) — use as_rx(val) instead.

docs.title: Dependency Tracking
docs.text: Computed now tracks its dependencies automatically at runtime — no need to declare them upfront. Values are only recomputed when actually read, and if a recomputed value turns out to be unchanged, downstream computeds won't needlessly re-run.

docs.title: Change Detection
docs.text:
Signified is smarter about deciding when a Signal's value has actually changed:

  • Functions are compared by identity rather than equality.
  • Arrays are compared element-by-element.
  • Assigning NaN to a signal that already holds NaN is treated as no change.

Mutating a signal's contents (e.g. setting an attribute or index) now also correctly invalidates downstream computeds, and unref/deep_unref align with how dependencies are tracked at runtime.

docs.title: rx namespace
docs.text:
Added Signal.rx namespace which includes several methods:

  • map (new) - lazy transform helper for derived values.
  • peek (new) - lazy pass-through side-effect helper (observational effects).
  • effect (new) - eager side-effect subscription with explicit dispose().
  • len (new)
  • is_ (new)
  • is_not
  • in_ (new)
  • contains
  • eq
  • where
  • as_bool

docs.title: Bug Fixes
docs.text: Fixed a bug in the IPython/Jupyter display integration where display observers could be garbage-collected before they had a chance to update.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
Added an interactive Playground to the docs, powered by Pyodide and CodeMirror, so you can try signified right in your browser.

Deprecations

Deprecated functions:

  • Computed(..., dependencies=...) — the dependencies argument is now ignored. Dependencies are automatically inferred from reactive reads during evaluation.
  • @reactive_method(...) — use @computed instead. Any dependency-name arguments are also ignored.

Deprecated several methods

  • x.as_bool(...) - Will eventually be removed entirely. Use computed(bool)(x) instead.
  • x.contains(...) - Use x.rx.contains instead.
  • x.eq(...) - Use x.rx.eq instead
  • x.where(...) - Use x.rx.where instead
  • x.is_not(...) - Use x.rx.is_not instead

• Significantly improved type inference across a wide range of methods.
  • Plugins are now disabled by default — set SIGNIFIED_ENABLE_HOOKS=1 to re-enable them.
  • Several performance improvements.
  • Expanded documentation.
  • Migrated CI to uv.

Breaking Changes

  • Plugins are now disabled by default.
  • OrderedSet and OrderedWeakRefSet have been renamed to _OrderedSet and _OrderedWeakRefSet. These were always internal types.

• Fixed packaging so NumPy is truly optional.
  • Fixed Python 3.14 compatibility.
  • Expanded the CI test matrix to cover newer Python versions.

• Improved weak-reference handling in the reactive observer internals.
  • Updated core/type integration around weakref sets.
  • Minor release metadata updates.

• Made IPython an optional dependency.
  • Removed the hard NumPy dependency from the base install.
  • Updated core/display logic to handle optional imports.

• Fixed a runtime typing issue for generic forward references (ReactiveValue/HasValue).
  • Added and expanded API documentation pages and updated MkDocs configuration.
  • Updated docs deployment workflow.

• Refactored the implementation into smaller, focused modules: core, ops, display, types, and utils.
  • Removed the old monolithic layout.
  • Updated docs and test scaffolding to match.

• Fixed deep_unref to avoid coercing unknown iterables into lists.
  • Minor packaging and version metadata adjustments.

• Added a plugin system (signified.plugins) with examples.
  • Added deep_unref, memory/performance improvements via __slots__, and typing improvements.
  • Substantially expanded docs: usage guides, limitations, plugin docs, changelog, and theme updates.

• Major expansion of the core reactive implementation and type-inference coverage.
  • Improved observe/unobserve and change-detection robustness.
  • Release and docs workflow improvements.

• Repackaged the project into a src/signified/ layout.
  • Ensured py.typed is included in the package.
  • Minor README and metadata cleanup.

• Improved README and docs landing content.
  • Fixed MkDocs configuration issues.
  • Minor source and metadata tweaks.

• Added support for Python 3.9+.
  • Added broad tests for signals, computed values, reactive methods, and type inference.
  • Added CI test workflow and moved to a src/ layout.

• Fixed package naming and docs after the project rename.
  • Updated project URLs and version metadata.
  • Updated changelog entries for the rename transition.
• Initial tagged release as signified.

docs.title: Library comparison
docs.text: Signified works much like the signals in many JavaScript frameworks: a calculation follows the values it reads, recalculates only when needed, and effects handle actions. This page shows how it lines up with other libraries, so you can tell what carries over when moving code or ideas between them.

docs.title: Python libraries
docs.text:
In each row, x starts at 1 and doubled calculates twice its value. Imports are omitted.

Library Create Read / write Calculate Signified x = Signal(1) x.value / x.value = 2 doubled = x * 2 reaktiv x = signal(1) x() / x.set(2) doubled = computed(lambda: x() * 2) Param x = rx(1) x.rx.value / x.rx.value = 2 doubled = x * 2

reaktiv is the closest match. Like Signified, it follows the values a function reads, caches results until an input changes, and runs effects immediately. It reads by calling x() instead of using operators, compares every value with is, prints effect errors instead of raising them, and offers async helpers and locking for graphs shared across threads.

Param builds reactive expressions differently: rx records the operations you apply and the values you pass in, rather than following reads inside a function. Its watchers subscribe to named parameters. If you already use Param parameters, its expressions connect directly to that model.

  • Param: building or inspecting an rx pipeline can run some steps early. Param does not compare results, so an unchanged result still notifies.

"Counts as unchanged" decides whether anything downstream updates. In every library above except Param, a calculation that recalculates to an unchanged result stops the update there.

docs.title: Where Signified differs
docs.text:
• Equality. Built-in scalars such as int, float, and str compare by value; everything else compares by identity, and Signified never calls an object's __eq__ unless you pass equal=. reaktiv uses is everywhere, and the JavaScript libraries use === or Object.is.
  • Nested reactive values stay as they are. A signal holding another signal returns that signal, not its value. Read it with unref, deep_unref, or a Binding. Vue, by contrast, unwraps refs inside reactive objects for you.
  • Binding. A binding is one stable handle whose source you can swap. Angular's linkedSignal, Svelte's writable $derived, and Vue and MobX computed setters solve related problems, but each writes or overrides values rather than switching sources.
  • Operators. Like Param, Python operators build calculations, so price * quantity is already reactive.
  • Errors. A failed calculation saves its exception and raises it on each read until an input changes. When effects fail, the rest still run and the errors are raised together. reaktiv and MobX log effect errors instead, and Vue, Svelte, and Solid send them to framework error handlers.
  • Synchronous, one thread at a time. Reads are tracked only while a function runs, never across await. Separate graphs can run on separate threads, but each graph is used from one thread at a time.

If you need every event in order, rather than the latest value, an event-stream library such as ReactiveX for Python is a better fit. Signals can skip intermediate values that nothing read.

Other libraries' behavior was checked against their documentation and source on September 19, 2026, using their default options.

docs.title: How updates work
docs.text: This page describes the rules behind Signified's updates. For an introduction with everyday examples, start with the usage guide.

docs.title: Which reads trigger updates
docs.text:
A computation or effect follows the reactive values it reads while running. These inputs are called its dependencies. After each run, only the inputs read during that run remain dependencies. In a conditional expression, that means the selected branch is tracked.

computed and effect read direct reactive arguments once per run. Other arguments, including lists and dictionaries, pass through unchanged:

from signified import Signal, computed

x = Signal(2)
config = {"x": x}

@computed
def double(config):
    return config["x"].value * 2

result = double(config)
assert result.value == 4
x.value = 3
assert result.value == 6

Reading x.value makes result follow x. Simply returning config would not.

Keep computed functions free of actions such as changing application state. An unread calculation may never run. Its read-only .value property also does not prevent changes to a list or object returned by the function.

docs.title: What counts as a change
docs.text:
Signal assignments and calculated results use the same rules:

  • Exact built-in int, bool, str, bytes, complex, NoneType, and float values compare by value. Two float NaNs count as unchanged.
  • Different types count as changed, including 1 versus True.
  • Everything else, including containers, arrays, subclasses of those built-ins, and user objects, compares by identity: only the same object is unchanged. Signified does not call these objects' equality methods.
  • When a value is unchanged, the previously stored object is kept.

A new dictionary therefore counts as a change even if it has the same contents. To compare by contents, pass an equal(old, new) function as equal= to Signal or Computed, or call x.rx.with_equal(equal) on a value built by an operator or @computed. It is called only when the rules above report a change, so it can make more values count as unchanged, never fewer. See Skip updates for equal contents.

Changing an existing dictionary through .value does not send an update. Replace it, call Signal.update() after changing it, or assign through the signal with state[key] = value. The container examples show all three approaches. Attribute assignment through a signal works the same way; a Computed or Binding does not forward these writes.

A computation or effect can skip running when its calculated inputs refresh to unchanged results. Switching a binding to an equal-valued source follows this rule too. Signal.update() and Computed.invalidate() explicitly send a change notification from that object.

docs.title: Nested values
docs.text:
A signal can hold another reactive value, and a calculation can return one. Neither reads it for you:

from signified import Binding, Computed, Signal, unref

inner = Signal(1)
outer = Signal(inner)
assert outer.value is inner
assert unref(outer) is inner
assert Computed(lambda: inner).value is inner
assert Binding(inner).value == 1
assert Binding(outer).value is inner

unref, Binding, operators, and decorated functions all read one level at a time. For example, (outer + 1).value is a Computed, because outer holds a signal. Use Binding(inner) + 1 to calculate from the number instead.

To read reactive values inside lists, dictionaries, and other containers, call deep_unref inside the computation or effect. Calling it beforehand gives you the data, but the callback will not follow the original values. See Nested values for supported types, JSON, and custom handlers.

docs.title: Read without adding a dependency
docs.text:
Use untracked() for incidental reads that should not trigger the surrounding computation or effect:

from signified import Computed, Effect, Signal, untracked

trigger, other = Signal(0), Signal(1)
derived = Computed(lambda: other.value * 2)
seen = []

def observe():
    current = trigger.value
    with untracked():
        seen.append((current, derived.value))

watcher = Effect(observe)
other.value = 2
assert seen == [(0, 2)]
trigger.value = 1
assert seen[-1] == (1, 4)
watcher.dispose()

The effect follows trigger, but not derived or other. The nested calculation derived still tracks its own inputs and returns its current value. Blocks can nest, and tracking resumes when a block exits, even after an error.

rx.tap(fn) serves a different purpose: it calls fn when its calculated value is evaluated and passes the value through. Cached reads do not repeat the call, and unread intermediate values are skipped.

docs.title: Batching and effect lifetime
docs.text:
batch() delays effects until the outermost batch exits. Writes take effect immediately, and reading a computed value inside the batch returns its current result. The usage guide has an example.

Outside a batch, effects run before the triggering update returns, after all calculations affected by that update have been marked for refresh. Multiple pending notifications can share a run. An effect that writes another value can cause further runs, so do not rely on effect order or assume each effect runs only once. Before rerunning an effect, Signified refreshes its calculated inputs; if all tracked inputs are unchanged, the callback is skipped.

Keep a reference to each effect while it should remain active. Pending work does not keep it alive. .dispose() cancels pending work, can be called from inside the callback, and is safe to call more than once. An effect created inside a batch waits for the batch to exit even for its first run; if discarded before then, it may never run.

Batching does not hide intermediate values or undo changes. If the batch body raises an error, applied writes remain and pending effects still run.

Each thread tracks reads, batches, and runs effects on its own. Separate graphs can run on separate threads at the same time, and a graph built on one thread can be used on another afterwards. Use one graph from one thread at a time: reading a Computed while another thread is computing it raises RuntimeError. batch() and untracked() apply to the thread that enters them; they are synchronous blocks and must not contain await.

docs.title: Errors and recovery
docs.text:
A Computed saves an ordinary exception the same way it saves a value:

from signified import Computed, Signal

divisor = Signal(0)
ratio = Computed(lambda: 10 / divisor.value)
try:
    ratio.value
except ZeroDivisionError:
    print("failed")  # failed
divisor.value = 2
print(ratio.value)  # 5.0

Reading ratio again raises the saved error without rerunning the function, until an input changes or you call .invalidate(). A failed run still follows the inputs it read before the error, which is how changing divisor lets ratio recover. For anything that reads ratio, each new failure counts as a change, and so does recovering, even to the last successful value.

When an effect raises, the other pending effects still run. A single failure is raised as-is; several are raised together as an ExceptionGroup. This also applies inside a batch. If the batch body raises as well, its error is grouped with the effect errors, in a BaseExceptionGroup when needed.

Exceptions that are not Exception subclasses, such as KeyboardInterrupt, are never saved. They stop and discard the pending effects, which still respond to later changes. If one effect runs more than 100 times in a single round of updates, usually because effects keep changing each other's inputs, Signified raises RuntimeError and discards the remaining work.

docs.title: Three ways to create an effect
docs.text:
Create an Effect object, decorate a function with @effect, or call .rx.effect() on a reactive value.

examples/effects/basics.py
"""Three ways to create an effect.

Run with: uv run examples/effects/basics.py
"""

from signified import Effect, Signal, effect


@effect
def log_count(value: int, label: str) -> None:
    # A Signal argument arrives as its current value on each run. Other
    # arguments, like label, pass through unchanged.
    print(f"{label}: {value}")


def example() -> None:
    count = Signal(0)

    print("1: Create an Effect object directly:")
    observer = Effect(lambda: print(f"Effect: {count.value}"))
    try:
        count.value = 1
        count.value = 1  # Unchanged scalar values do not trigger another run.
    finally:
        observer.dispose()

    print("\n2: Use the @effect decorator:")
    logger = log_count(count, "@effect")
    try:
        count.value = 2
    finally:
        logger.dispose()

    print("\n3: Use .rx.effect():")
    display = count.rx.effect(lambda value: print(f"rx.effect: {value}"))
    try:
        count.value = 3
    finally:
        display.dispose()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    example()

docs.title: Save settings when they change
docs.text:
An effect writes settings to a file, and batch() combines related edits into one save.

examples/effects/autosave.py
"""Save application settings when they change, combining related edits.

Run with: uv run examples/effects/autosave.py
"""

import json
from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

from signified import Signal, batch, effect


@effect
def save_settings(settings_path: Path, current_theme: str, current_font_size: int) -> None:
    settings = {"theme": current_theme, "font_size": current_font_size}
    # write_text opens and closes the file on each run.
    settings_path.write_text(json.dumps(settings, indent=2) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
    print(f"Saved {settings}")


def example() -> None:
    theme = Signal("light")
    font_size = Signal(14)

    with TemporaryDirectory(prefix="signified-settings-") as temporary:
        settings_path = Path(temporary) / "settings.json"
        saver = save_settings(settings_path, theme, font_size)  # Saves the initial settings.
        try:
            # Both writes produce a single save with the final settings.
            with batch():
                theme.value = "dark"
                font_size.value = 18

            font_size.value = 20  # Saves synchronously before this line returns.
        finally:
            saver.dispose()

        theme.value = "light"  # No save after disposal.
        print("\nLast saved settings:")
        print(settings_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"), end="")
        # The temporary directory is removed when this example exits.


if __name__ == "__main__":
    example()

docs.title: Follow the selected sensor
docs.text:
@tracked_fields makes a dataclass's attributes reactive, so a display follows whichever sensor is selected.

examples/effects/dashboard.py
"""Batch updates and follow only the selected sensor's readings.

`Sensors` is an ordinary dataclass. `@tracked_fields` makes its attributes
reactive: a calculation or effect that reads `sensors.primary` runs again when
`sensors.primary` is reassigned. Writes are plain attribute assignments.

- `select_sensors` is a calculation that reads whichever sensor is in use. It
  takes the whole `sensors` object and reads its fields inside, so it follows
  them. Passing `sensors.primary` instead would pass today's number, which
  never changes.
- `render` is an effect that prints the selected reading with its label. It
  runs again whenever either one changes.
- `batch()` groups several writes into one update.

Expected output:

    Temperature: 20 C

    Batch writes into one display update:
    Temperature: 22 C

    Rename the display:
    Office: 22 C

    Switch to the backup sensor:
    Office: 16 C
    The primary sensor is no longer a dependency:
    Office: 19 C

Run with: uv run examples/effects/dashboard.py
"""

from dataclasses import dataclass

from signified import Effect, batch, computed, tracked_fields


@tracked_fields
@dataclass(slots=True)
class Sensors:
    primary: int = 20
    backup: int = 18
    use_backup: bool = False
    label: str = "Temperature"


@computed
def select_sensors(sensors: Sensors) -> int:
    return sensors.backup if sensors.use_backup else sensors.primary


def example() -> None:
    sensors = Sensors()
    selected = select_sensors(sensors)

    def render() -> None:
        print(f"{sensors.label}: {selected.value} C")

    # Note: we hold a reference to effect so that it doesn't get
    # immediately garbage collected.
    display = Effect(render)  # Temperature: 20 C  # noqa

    print("\nBatch writes into one display update:")
    with batch():
        sensors.primary = 22
        sensors.backup = 16

    print("\nRename the display:")
    sensors.label = "Office"  # Office: 22 C

    print("\nSwitch to the backup sensor:")
    sensors.use_backup = True  # Office: 16 C
    print("The primary sensor is no longer a dependency:")
    sensors.primary = 99  # No display update.
    sensors.backup = 19  # Office: 19 C


if __name__ == "__main__":
    example()

docs.title: Rebuild an index when files change
docs.text:
A file watcher updates a signal, and an effect rewrites index.md only when the notes' titles change. This one needs watchdog.

example.pyhelper.py examples/effects/notes_index/example.py
"""Rebuild an index of Markdown notes whenever the notes folder changes.

`helper.py` creates a temporary notes folder and plays the part of you editing
it. This file only watches the folder and reacts:

- `notes` is a signal holding each note's text. Whenever anything in the
  folder changes, the watcher re-reads the folder into `notes`.
- `table_of_contents` is a calculation that lists each note's title.
- `write_index` is an effect that writes the table of contents to `index.md`.
  It is the only code that changes anything outside the program.

Editing a note's body without changing its title produces the same table of
contents, so `write_index` does not run and `index.md` is left alone.

The watcher runs on its own thread, so `notes` changes and `write_index` runs
there. That is fine because nothing else uses these values while the edits
happen: Signified needs each set of connected values used by one thread at a
time. If other code also used `notes` while watching, you would pass the
watcher's events to that code's thread, for example through a queue.

Expected output:

    Wrote index.md:
    - Groceries (groceries.md)
    - Ideas (ideas.md)

    Adding travel.md
    Wrote index.md:
    - Groceries (groceries.md)
    - Ideas (ideas.md)
    - Travel plans (travel.md)

    Adding eggs to groceries.md

    Renaming Ideas to Project ideas
    Wrote index.md:
    - Groceries (groceries.md)
    - Project ideas (ideas.md)
    - Travel plans (travel.md)

Run with: uv run --with watchdog examples/effects/notes_index/example.py
"""

from pathlib import Path

from helper import edit_notes, notes_folder
from watchdog.events import FileSystemEvent, FileSystemEventHandler
from watchdog.observers.polling import PollingObserver

from signified import Signal, computed, effect


def read_notes(folder: Path) -> dict[str, str]:
    return {path.name: path.read_text() for path in sorted(folder.glob("*.md"))}


@computed
def table_of_contents(notes: dict[str, str]) -> str:
    titles = {name: text.splitlines()[0].removeprefix("# ") for name, text in notes.items()}
    return "\n".join(f"- {title} ({name})" for name, title in titles.items())


@effect
def write_index(toc: str, path: Path) -> None:
    path.write_text(toc + "\n")
    print(f"Wrote {path.name}:\n{toc}")


class UpdateNotes(FileSystemEventHandler):
    """Re-read the folder into `notes` whenever anything in it changes."""

    def __init__(self, folder: Path, notes: Signal[dict[str, str]]) -> None:
        self.folder = folder
        self.notes = notes

    def on_any_event(self, event: FileSystemEvent) -> None:
        self.notes.value = read_notes(self.folder)


def example() -> None:
    with notes_folder() as folder:
        notes = Signal(read_notes(folder))
        writer = write_index(table_of_contents(notes), folder.parent / "index.md")

        # Polling works on every OS; native macOS notifications can go missing.
        observer = PollingObserver(timeout=0.1)
        observer.schedule(UpdateNotes(folder, notes), str(folder))
        observer.start()
        try:
            edit_notes(folder)
        finally:
            observer.stop()
            observer.join()
            writer.dispose()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    example()
examples/effects/notes_index/helper.py
"""Stand in for a person editing notes, so the example runs unattended.

Nothing here uses Signified.
"""

import time
from collections.abc import Generator
from contextlib import contextmanager
from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory


@contextmanager
def notes_folder() -> Generator[Path]:
    """Create a temporary folder with two notes. It is deleted on exit."""
    with TemporaryDirectory() as temporary:
        folder = Path(temporary, "notes")
        folder.mkdir()
        (folder / "groceries.md").write_text("# Groceries\n- milk\n")
        (folder / "ideas.md").write_text("# Ideas\n- a reactive to-do app\n")
        yield folder


def edit_notes(folder: Path) -> None:
    """Add a note, change one's body, and retitle another.

    Pauses half a second before each edit and after the last, so a watcher has
    time to notice each one.
    """
    edits = [
        ("Adding travel.md", "travel.md", "# Travel plans\n- book flights\n"),
        ("Adding eggs to groceries.md", "groceries.md", "# Groceries\n- milk\n- eggs\n"),
        ("Renaming Ideas to Project ideas", "ideas.md", "# Project ideas\n- a reactive to-do app\n"),
    ]
    for message, name, text in edits:
        time.sleep(0.5)
        print(f"\n{message}")
        (folder / name).write_text(text)
    time.sleep(0.5)

docs.title: Count reads and writes
docs.text:
A plugin that records how often each reactive value is read and changed.

examples/plugins/access_tracker.py
"""Count reads and writes of each reactive value with a plugin.

Run with: uv run examples/plugins/access_tracker.py
"""

import datetime
import time
from collections import defaultdict
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from enum import Enum, auto
from typing import Any
from weakref import WeakValueDictionary

from signified import Signal, Variable
from signified.plugins import hookimpl, plugin_manager


class EventType(Enum):
    READ = auto()
    WRITE = auto()
    CREATE = auto()


@dataclass
class AccessEvent:
    """Represents a single access to a reactive value."""

    timestamp: datetime.datetime
    event_type: EventType
    value: Any


@dataclass
class AccessStats:
    read_count: int = 0
    write_count: int = 0
    creation_time: datetime.datetime = field(default_factory=datetime.datetime.now)
    last_access_time: datetime.datetime = field(default_factory=datetime.datetime.now)
    value_history: list[AccessEvent] = field(default_factory=list, repr=False)

    def add_event(self, event_type: EventType, value: Any = None) -> None:
        now = datetime.datetime.now()

        if event_type == EventType.READ:
            self.read_count += 1
            self.last_access_time = now
        elif event_type in (EventType.WRITE, EventType.CREATE):
            if event_type == EventType.WRITE:
                self.write_count += 1
            elif event_type == EventType.CREATE:
                self.creation_time = now
            self.last_access_time = now
            self.value_history.append(AccessEvent(now, event_type, value))

    @property
    def total_accesses(self) -> int:
        """Total number of reads and modifications."""
        return self.read_count + self.write_count

    @property
    def last_value(self) -> Any:
        """Most recently recorded value."""
        return self.value_history[-1].value if self.value_history else None


class AccessTracker:
    """Plugin for tracking reactive value access patterns.

    History records the internal cached value without invoking read hooks or
    evaluating lazy computations. A Computed's creation value is its initial
    None placeholder; its evaluated value is recorded by the updated hook.
    """

    def __init__(self):
        self.stats: dict[int, AccessStats] = defaultdict(AccessStats)
        self._variables: WeakValueDictionary[int, Variable[Any]] = WeakValueDictionary()

    def cleanup(self) -> None:
        """Clear stats."""
        self.stats.clear()
        self._variables.clear()

    @hookimpl
    def created(self, value: Variable[Any]) -> None:
        """Track creation of new reactive values."""
        self.stats[id(value)].add_event(EventType.CREATE, value._value)
        self._variables[id(value)] = value

    @hookimpl
    def updated(self, value: Variable[Any]) -> None:
        """Track modifications to reactive values."""
        self.stats[id(value)].add_event(EventType.WRITE, value._value)

    @hookimpl
    def read(self, value: Variable[Any]) -> None:
        """Record a read access to a reactive value."""
        self.stats[id(value)].add_event(EventType.READ)

    def get_stats(self, value: Variable[Any]) -> AccessStats:
        """Get access statistics for a specific reactive value."""
        return self.stats[id(value)]

    def print_summary(self) -> None:
        """Print summary statistics for all tracked values."""
        print("\nAccess Pattern Summary:")
        print("-" * 50)
        for value_id, stats in self.stats.items():
            value = self._variables.get(value_id)
            print(f"Value {value:n}:")
            print(f"\tReads: {stats.read_count}")
            print(f"\tModifications: {stats.write_count}")
            print(f"\tTotal accesses: {stats.total_accesses}")
            if stats.creation_time and stats.last_access_time:
                lifetime = stats.last_access_time - stats.creation_time
                print(f"\tLifetime: {lifetime.total_seconds():.2f} seconds")
            print()


tracker = AccessTracker()
plugin_manager.register(tracker)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    x = Signal(1).with_name("x")
    y = Signal(2).with_name("y")
    time.sleep(0.1)

    x.value = 10
    y.value = 20
    x.value = 30

    z = (x + y).with_name("z")
    _ = z.value  # Reads z, which reads x and y as it calculates.
    time.sleep(0.1)

    tracker.print_summary()
    print(f"Value history for x: {[v.value for v in tracker.get_stats(x).value_history]}")
    print(f"Value history for y: {[v.value for v in tracker.get_stats(y).value_history]}")
    print(f"Value history for z: {[v.value for v in tracker.get_stats(z).value_history]}")

    plugin_manager.unregister(tracker)
    tracker.cleanup()

docs.text:
<, <=, >, and >= produce reactive results.

== and != do not. Comparisons between reactive objects use identity, so they remain usable as distinct keys in sets and dictionaries. To compare wrapped values reactively, use x.rx.eq(y) or x.rx.ne(y).

Use .rx for the following operations:

To calculate… Use Value equality x.rx.eq(y) Value inequality x.rx.ne(y) Object identity x.rx.is_(y), x.rx.is_not(y) Membership x.rx.in_(items), items.rx.contains(x) Truthiness x.rx.as_bool() Length items.rx.len() A conditional result condition.rx.where(when_true, when_false)

==, !=, is, in, bool(x), and len(x) do not create these reactive calculations. Python's if, and, and or also do not build reactive expressions. Use .rx.where(...) to choose between values, or put ordinary Python branching inside a Computed function that reads .value.

docs.title: Object and container access
docs.text:
x.name, x[key], and x(...) create calculated values. Methods can be chained, for example text.strip().lower().

Only Signal forwards writes such as x.name = value, x[key] = value, and del x[key] to its stored object and sends updates. Attribute names must already exist. Item assignment and deletion support wrapped lists and dictionaries. Changes through the raw .value need an explicit .update() call; see Lists and dictionaries.

docs.title: Complete API reference
docs.text: See the operator API for individual methods and the rx API for additional operations.

docs.title: Migrating to 0.6
docs.text: Version 0.6 no longer reads reactive values stored inside other values, such as a signal held by a signal or a list of signals; your code reads them explicitly. It also changes how equality, effects, and errors work. After upgrading, check both your results and how they update when inputs change.

docs.title: Prepare on 0.5.1 first
docs.text:
You can make these changes before upgrading:

  • Enable migration warnings while exercising representative workflows.
  • Read .value when a function should return a reactive object's current value.
  • Call deep_unref inside callbacks that need values from nested containers.
  • Register custom containers with deep_unref.register(Type).
  • Replace rx.peek(fn) with rx.tap(fn).
  • Make changes through the Signal that owns the value.

Binding, batch(), and untracked() require 0.6. Version 0.5.1 still reads nested values for you and keeps the old equality and effect timing rules, so test those behaviors again after upgrading, even if no warnings appear.

docs.title: Following versus storing
docs.text:
Replace Signal(source) with Binding(source) when the outer object should follow another signal's value:

from signified import Binding, Signal

source = Signal(1)
# Before 0.6: selected = Signal(source)
selected = Binding(source)
source.value = 2
assert selected.value == 2

In 0.6, Signal(source) stores the source object itself. Likewise, Computed(lambda: source) returns that object. Change it to Computed(lambda: source.value) to calculate from its current value.

unref and Binding read one reactive object at a time. If that object's value is another reactive object, it is returned as-is. For more on replacing sources, see Binding.

docs.title: Container arguments and serialization
docs.text:
Decorated functions previously resolved reactive values inside container arguments for you. Move that work inside the function:

from signified import Signal, computed, deep_unref

values = [Signal(1), Signal(2)]
# Before 0.6: total = computed(sum)(values)
total = computed(lambda items: sum(deep_unref(items)))(values)
assert total.value == 3
values[0].value = 10
assert total.value == 12

Direct reactive arguments are still read automatically. deep_unref remains supported, with the handler API introduced in 0.5.1. Calling it before creating the computation does not make that computation follow the original inputs.

Unregistered iterables now pass through unchanged. Register your exact custom type if you need its contents resolved. Colliding keys or set members now raise an error instead of silently losing data. See Nested values for registration, JSON, supported containers, and copying limits.

docs.title: Equality and mutation
docs.text:
Review code that relied on equal lists, dictionaries, or arrays suppressing updates. These now compare by object identity, so a new object counts as a change even if its contents are equal. Exact built-in scalar values still compare by value; see the full equality rules.

Effects can now skip running when their calculated inputs return unchanged results, including when a binding switches to an equal-valued source. If an effect must react to the original signal's changes, read that signal as well.

Only Signal forwards attribute and item writes. Change the owning signal instead of writing through a Computed or Binding. Unknown attribute names now raise AttributeError. Raw object changes still need an explicit .update(); see Lists and dictionaries.

docs.title: Batch writes and untracked reads
docs.text:
Review code that assumes effects run once per write, in a fixed order, or again after every failed read:

  • batch() defers effects until its outermost block exits, including the first run of an effect created inside the block. Writes are still immediate.
  • One effect can cause further runs by changing another value. Batching does not undo writes on error or provide thread safety.
  • A Computed now saves an ordinary exception until an input changes or .invalidate() is called. Repeated reads raise the same saved error without rerunning the function. New failed evaluations and recovery count as changes.
  • Other pending effects continue after an ordinary effect failure. Multiple failures are raised together as an ExceptionGroup; use except* to handle them when needed.

See How updates work for lifetime, error recovery, and combined batch errors.

rx.peek(fn) is removed. Use rx.tap(fn) to inspect a calculation when it runs, or untracked() to read without adding a dependency. tap saves its result and skips unread intermediate values; it is not an automatic effect.

docs.title: Optional migration diagnostics
docs.text:
Warnings are available in 0.5.1 and 0.6, and removed in 0.7. Run them on one of those versions before upgrading further:

from signified import migration

migration.enable_warnings()
# Or wrap the code being checked in: with migration.warnings():

You can also set SIGNIFIED_MIGRATION_WARNINGS=1 before import. To make warnings fail your tests:

SIGNIFIED_MIGRATION_WARNINGS=1 pytest -W error::signified.migration.SignifiedMigrationWarning

Warnings flag reactive values stored in signals, returned from computations, or passed inside containers to decorated functions. Checking does not read reactive values or consume iterators, and a Binding following a reactive source does not warn.

Warnings can miss reactive values hidden inside your own objects, and they also flag signals you store on purpose. They say nothing about equality, effect timing, or forwarded writes, so review those separately. Turn warnings off once you are done.
