docs.title: Writing plugins
docs.text: Plugins let you log or inspect reads and changes to reactive values. Signified calls your plugin's methods when these events happen.

docs.title: Enable plugins
docs.text: Hooks run while at least one plugin is registered with plugin_manager, as shown below. With no plugin registered, reactive values skip them.

docs.title: Available hooks
docs.text:
Each hook receives the reactive object as its value argument:

Hook When it runs created A reactive value is created. read Its current value is read. updated It sends a change notification. named It is given a name.

docs.title: Create and register a plugin
docs.text:
Implement the hooks you need with @hookimpl, then register the instance. A plugin can also be a module of @hookimpl functions. This plugin counts new reactive values:

from typing import Any

from signified import Signal, Variable
from signified.plugins import hookimpl, plugin_manager

class CreationCounter:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.count = 0

    @hookimpl
    def created(self, value: Variable[Any]) -> None:
        self.count += 1
        print(f"Created {value:d}")  # :d shows the object's type and ID.

plugin = CreationCounter()
plugin_manager.register(plugin)

x = Signal(1)
y = x + 1
print(plugin.count)  # 2

plugin_manager.unregister(plugin)

Use logging in place of print if your application already has logging set up. Unregister the plugin when you no longer need it. For a larger example, see the access tracker, which counts reads and writes for each reactive value.

When several plugins implement the same hook, the most recently registered one runs first. register raises an error if the plugin is already registered, if an @hookimpl method's name is not one of the hooks above, or if it does not accept a value argument.

docs.title: Resolving nested values
docs.text:
Use deep_unref to replace signals, computed values, and bindings inside containers with their current values:

from signified import Signal, deep_unref

payload = {"position": [Signal(10), Signal(20)]}
assert deep_unref(payload) == {"position": [10, 20]}

docs.title: Save or send data as JSON
docs.text:
Read nested values before passing data to a serializer. Keep that read inside an effect if the output should follow changes:

import json
from signified import Effect, Signal, deep_unref

x, y = Signal(1), Signal(2)
payload = {"position": [x, y]}
sent = []
watcher = Effect(lambda: sent.append(json.dumps(deep_unref(payload))))
assert json.loads(sent[-1]) == {"position": [1, 2]}
x.value = 3
assert json.loads(sent[-1]) == {"position": [3, 2]}
watcher.dispose()

For a one-time result, use json.dumps(deep_unref(payload)) directly. deep_unref only reads reactive values; dates and custom objects still need conversion to a format your serializer accepts.

docs.title: Custom objects
docs.text:
Register a function to tell deep_unref how to rebuild your own type. Use the supplied resolve function on each field you want to read:

from dataclasses import dataclass
from signified import ResolveContext, Signal, deep_unref

@dataclass
class Position:
    x: float | Signal[float]
    y: float | Signal[float]

@deep_unref.register(Position)
def resolve_position(position: Position, resolve: ResolveContext) -> Position:
    return Position(x=resolve(position.x), y=resolve(position.y))

position = Position(Signal(10.0), Signal(20.0))
plain = deep_unref({"position": position})
assert plain == {"position": Position(x=10.0, y=20.0)}
assert isinstance(position.x, Signal)  # The input is unchanged.

Choose which fields to resolve and which to copy unchanged. Prefer returning a new object rather than changing the input. Use the supplied resolve instead of calling deep_unref again so the same registered handlers are used throughout.

Registration applies to the exact type; register subclasses separately. Registering another handler for that type replaces the previous one. Handlers can return a different type, so deep_unref results are typed as Any. See the API reference for signatures.

docs.title: Supported values
docs.text:
• Built-in lists, tuples, dictionaries (keys and values), sets, frozensets, and collections.deque objects are rebuilt. Subclasses need their own handlers.
  • With NumPy installed, arrays containing Python objects are rebuilt with their shape and dtype preserved. Numeric arrays pass through unchanged. Array subclasses need their own handlers.
  • Unknown objects pass through unchanged, without being inspected or iterated. They may still contain reactive values or share mutable data with the input.
  • Each occurrence is resolved independently, including calls to custom handlers. Two references to one container become separate rebuilt containers.
  • Cycles eventually raise RecursionError. Duplicate keys or set members after resolution raise ValueError; unhashable keys or members raise TypeError. Errors from handlers pass through unchanged.

The result is not necessarily an independent copy, serializable data, or a snapshot taken at a single instant. Reads inside a computation or effect track only the reactive values reached during traversal.

docs.title: Upgrading custom containers
docs.text: In 0.6, unregistered iterable types pass through unchanged. Add a handler like the one above if you relied on automatic traversal. See Migrating to 0.6.

docs.title: Type checkers
docs.text:
Use Pyright for the best type inference with Signified. Pyrefly is a usable alternative with caveats.

Assessed on 2026-10-10 with Python 3.14.3 and Signified 0.7.0 (revision 9de4e8b). The inference suite checks 765 inferred types and 60 operations that should be rejected.

Checker Version Wrong types (of 765) Invalid operations flagged (of 60) Recommendation Pyright 1.1.414 0 60 Recommended Pyrefly 1.3.2 33 42 Usable with caveats ty 0.0.86 247 56 Not recommended yet mypy 2.4.0 165 34 Not recommended
  • Pyrefly: abs, math.trunc, math.floor, and math.ceil on signals infer Unknown, and divmod infers the wrong type for mixed, Decimal, or reflected operands. It accepts round and the math functions on unsupported values, and reports an error when calling a wrapped callable object.
  • ty: unref and Binding rarely infer the right type, many operators infer Unknown, and some valid operations are rejected, such as Signal(10.0) // Signal(2.0).
  • mypy: unref and Binding reject valid arguments and infer Never. Operators on signals mostly infer correctly. Mypy ran with --check-untyped-defs so test bodies were checked.

Even with Pyright, attributes read through a signal, such as Signal(person).name, and deep_unref results are typed Any, so a misspelled attribute is not caught. Functions decorated with @computed or @effect keep their return type but do not check their arguments.

docs.title: Usage guide
docs.text: Start with a Signal for each value your application changes. Build calculations from those signals, then use effects for actions such as logging or updating a display.

docs.title: Signals and calculated values
docs.text:
Read a signal with .value and assign to .value to change it. Python operators create a Computed that follows its inputs:

from signified import Signal

price = Signal(10)
quantity = Signal(2)
total = price * quantity

print(total.value)  # 20   (an ordinary Python value)
quantity.value = 3
print(total.value)  # 30

A computed value is calculated when read and saved until an input changes. Its .value is read-only. You can use it in further calculations, such as with_tax = total * 1.2.

docs.title: Use your own functions
docs.text:
@computed makes a function return a Computed. Direct signal arguments are read for you, so the function receives their values:

from signified import Signal, computed

@computed
def average(values):
    return sum(values) / len(values)

numbers = Signal([2, 4, 6])
result = average(numbers)
print(result.value)  # 4.0
numbers.value = [10, 20]
print(result.value)  # 15.0

For an existing function, use computed(sum)(numbers) or numbers.rx.map(sum). Keep these functions focused on calculating a result; use an effect for work that should happen automatically.

docs.title: Run actions when values change
docs.text:
@effect runs a function immediately and again when the values it reads change. Keep the returned object while the effect should stay active, then call .dispose() to stop it:

from signified import Signal, effect

@effect
def show_total(total):
    print("Total:", total)

price = Signal(10)
quantity = Signal(2)
watcher = show_total(price * quantity)  # Total: 20
quantity.value = 3                     # Total: 30
watcher.dispose()
quantity.value = 4                     # No output

An effect that reads only a calculation skips running when that calculation recalculates to the same result. The effect examples show effects that refresh a display, autosave settings, and rebuild an index when files change.

docs.title: Group related changes
docs.text:
Use batch() to delay effects until a group of writes is finished:

from signified import Effect, Signal, batch

price, quantity = Signal(10), Signal(2)
watcher = Effect(lambda: print(price.value * quantity.value))  # 20
with batch():
    price.value = 12
    quantity.value = 3
# Prints 36 once the block exits.
watcher.dispose()

Values change immediately inside the block; batching does not undo writes if an error occurs. Use a graph from one thread at a time, and do not put await inside batch() or untracked().

Use untracked() when a read inside an effect or calculation should not make it run again when that value changes. See How updates work for an example, effect timing, and error handling.

docs.title: Lists and dictionaries
docs.text:
Reading an item through a signal creates a calculation. Assigning an item through the signal also tells dependent calculations to update:

from signified import Signal, computed

numbers = Signal([1, 2, 3])
first = numbers[0]
total = computed(sum)(numbers)

numbers[0] = 9
print(first.value)  # 9
print(total.value)  # 14

numbers.value.append(4)  # Changing the raw list does not send an update.
print(total.value)       # 14 (the saved result)
numbers.update()         # Tell Signified about the change.
print(total.value)       # 18

numbers.value = [5, 6]   # Replacing the list also sends an update.
print(total.value)       # 11

Dictionaries work the same way: settings["theme"] = "light" sends an update; settings.value["theme"] = "light" needs a subsequent settings.update(). Changes made through another reference to the raw object also need notification.

docs.title: Signals inside containers
docs.text:
A list or dictionary can contain signals. Merely storing them does not make calculations follow their values. Read the signals inside your function, or use deep_unref to read all of them:

from signified import Computed, Signal, deep_unref

values = [Signal(1), Signal(2)]
total = Computed(lambda: sum(deep_unref(values)))
print(total.value)  # 3
values[0].value = 10
print(total.value)  # 12

Keep deep_unref inside the function so its reads are tracked. The nested values guide covers supported containers, JSON, and custom objects.

docs.title: Skip updates for equal contents
docs.text:
A new list counts as a change even if its contents match the old one, because Signified compares lists, dictionaries, arrays, and your own objects by identity. Pass equal= to compare them your way:

from signified import Signal, effect

@effect
def show(point):
    print("Point:", point)

point = Signal([0, 0], equal=lambda old, new: old == new)
watcher = show(point)  # Point: [0, 0]
point.value = [0, 0]   # Same contents: no update
point.value = [1, 0]   # Point: [1, 0]
watcher.dispose()

When equal(old, new) returns True, the signal keeps the old object and nothing that depends on it updates. Computed accepts equal= too. For a value built with operators or @computed, set it afterwards with .rx.with_equal(), for example transform = (rotation @ scale).rx.with_equal(np.array_equal).

docs.title: Attributes and methods
docs.text:
You can read attributes and call methods through a signal:

from types import SimpleNamespace
from signified import Signal

person = Signal(SimpleNamespace(name="Alice"))
name = person.name
person.name = "Bob"
print(name.value)  # Bob

text = Signal("  Hello, World!  ")
message = text.strip().lower()
print(message.value)  # hello, world!

Only Signal forwards attribute and item writes to the object it holds. An attribute must already exist on that object. Method calls produce calculated values; calling a method that changes the raw object does not automatically send an update. For example, use numbers.value.append(4) followed by numbers.update() to change a list.

docs.title: Choose between values
docs.text:
Use .rx for operations that need a reactive alternative to Python syntax:

from signified import Signal

username = Signal(None)
message = username.rx.is_not(None).rx.where("Signed in", "Please log in")
print(message.value)  # Please log in
username.value = "admin"
print(message.value)  # Signed in

For a reactive equality check, use x.rx.eq(y). For reactive truthiness, use x.rx.as_bool(). The operator cheatsheet lists the other operations and their Python counterparts.

docs.title: Switch inputs with Binding
docs.text:
A Signal holds a value. A Binding can hold a value or follow another reactive value, and you can change which at any time. Calculations built from the binding keep working through every switch.

This suits an object's properties. A shape's x position might be a fixed number at first, then follow an animation later:

from signified import Binding, Signal

frame = Signal(0)
x = Binding(0)        # a plain number for now
label_x = x + 10      # e.g. a label that sits to the right of the shape

x.value = 5           # set a number, like a Signal
print(label_x.value)  # 15

x.value = frame * 2   # now follow an animation
frame.value = 30
print(label_x.value)  # 70

docs.title: Why not a Signal?
docs.text:
With x = Signal(0), there is no good way to make x follow frame * 2:

  • x.value = frame * 2 stores the Computed object itself. label_x.value becomes a Computed, not a number.
  • x.value = (frame * 2).value copies the current number once. x does not change again when frame does.
  • Rebuilding label_x from frame * 2 works, but anything still holding the old label_x, such as an effect or another object, is left behind.

A Binding gives the object one handle for its whole life, while you choose what drives it.

docs.title: Build on the current source
docs.text:
x.source returns whatever x currently follows. A binding can also follow another binding. To layer a new calculation on top of the current source, use .derive():

x.derive(lambda previous: previous + 100)  # shift whatever x was following
print(label_x.value)  # 170

Use previous inside that function. Referring to x would make the binding depend on itself. Direct self-binding is rejected; indirect loops raise when read.

docs.title: Track attribute reassignment
docs.text:
A calculation that reads unref(material.roughness) follows a signal stored in that attribute, but it cannot see the attribute itself being replaced. tracked_fields makes reassignment visible:

from dataclasses import dataclass
from signified import Computed, HasValue, Signal, tracked_fields, unref

@tracked_fields
@dataclass(slots=True)
class Material:
    roughness: HasValue[float] = 0.5

material = Material()
doubled = Computed(lambda: unref(material.roughness) * 2)
material.roughness = 0.25
print(doubled.value)  # 0.5
material.roughness = Signal(0.1)
print(doubled.value)  # 0.2

Reading the attribute returns exactly what was stored; it never unwraps. Assigning a signal replaces the stored one instead of writing into it. Pass names, as in @tracked_fields("roughness"), to track only some attributes, or to track attributes of a class that is not a dataclass. The dashboard example drives an effect from a tracked dataclass, with batching.

docs.title: Force a calculation to refresh
docs.text:
If a calculation reads through an ordinary Python object, Signified cannot see that object's attributes being replaced. For classes you control, use tracked_fields. Otherwise, call .invalidate() to recalculate on the next read:

from types import SimpleNamespace
from signified import Computed, Signal

holder = SimpleNamespace(source=Signal(5))
doubled = Computed(lambda: holder.source.value * 2)
print(doubled.value)  # 10
holder.source = Signal(20)
print(doubled.value)  # 10
doubled.invalidate()
print(doubled.value)  # 40

docs.title: More helpers
docs.text:
See the API reference for:

  • unref(value): accept either a plain value or a signal, computed value, or binding.
  • as_rx(value): wrap a plain value in a signal; leave reactive values unchanged.
  • has_value and is_reactive: check and narrow types.
  • Signal.at(value): temporarily change a value inside a with block.
  • x.rx.tap(fn): call fn with each newly calculated value (runs only when something reads the result).

For editor and type-checking support, see Type checkers.
